# A fiber-level layer-cake expansion inequality

This is an auxiliary lemma, not a proof of OC.

Let d>=1 and let A be a bounded compact subset of
(p+2 Z^n) x R^d, with positive mixed volume a. Write a_z=vol_d(A_z),
and let a_max=max_z a_z. Then

    vol_MI((A+A)/2) >= 2a-a_max.

Proof. Write G=(A+A)/2 and g_m=vol_d(G_m). Classical Brunn--Minkowski
on any two nonempty positive-volume fibers implies

    g_{(u+v)/2} >= ((a_u^(1/d)+a_v^(1/d))/2)^d >= min(a_u,a_v).

For t>0 put Z_t={z:a_z>=t}. This is finite. Whenever it is nonempty,

    #{m:g_m>=t} >= |(Z_t+Z_t)/2| >= 2|Z_t|-1.

The midpoint indices are integral by the common-parity assumption. For the
last inequality, choose a linear functional injective on Z_t and order its
points z_1,...,z_N. The sums

    2z_1,z_1+z_2,...,z_1+z_N,z_2+z_N,...,2z_N

have strictly increasing functional values and are 2N-1 distinct sums.
Integrating the counting inequality for 0<t<=a_max gives

    sum_m g_m >= integral_0^a_max (2|Z_t|-1)dt
               = 2 sum_z a_z-a_max.

All sums are finite, so the layer-cake interchange is elementary. QED.

If A is contained in an exclusive cap region of a convex body and that region
is closed under midpoint formation at integer indices, the left-hand side is
bounded above by the mixed volume of the same cap region. This turns the
lemma into a quantitative constraint on dispersed same-parity exclusive mass.
It does not by itself supply a lower bound on the amount of exclusive mass or
construct a common center.
